source_text: Οἱ γεωργοὶ δὲ, ταῖς ἀρούραις ἐπικαθήμενοι, καὶ τὰς χεῖρας κατὰ τῶν γονάτων συμπλέκοντες (τοῦτο δὴ τῶν πενθούν των τὸ σχῆμα), τοὺς ματαίους ἑαυτῶν πόνους δακρύουσι, πρὸς παῖδας νηπίους ἀφορῶντες, καὶ ὀδυρόμενοι· πρὸς γυναῖκας ἀτενίζοντες, καὶ θρηνοῦντες, ἐπαφώμενοι καὶ ψηλαφῶντες τοὺς ξηροὺς χόρτους τῶν γεννημάτων, ἀνοιμώζοντες δὲ μεγάλα, καθάπερ οἱ πατέρες οἱ τοὺς ἐν ἄνθει τῆς ἡλικίας υἱοὺς ἀπολέ σαντες. Λεγέσθω τοίνυν καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς παρὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ προφήτου, οὗ μικρὸν πρόσθεν ἐν προοιμίοις ἐμνημονεύσαμεν· Καὶ ἐγὼ, φησὶν, ἀνέσχον ἐξ ὑμῶν τὸν ὑετὸν πρὸ τριῶν μηνῶν τοῦ τρυγητοῦ· καὶ βρέξω ἐπὶ πόλιν μίαν, ἐπὶ δὲ πόλιν μίαν οὐ βρέξω· καὶ μερὶς μία βραχήσεται, καὶ μερὶς, ἐφ' ἣν οὐ βρέξω, ξηρανθήσεται. Καὶ συναθροί σονται δύο ἢ τρεῖς πόλεις εἰς μίαν, πιεῖν ὕδωρ, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐμπλησθῶσι· διότι οὐκ ἐπεστράφητε πρὸς μὲ, λέγει Κύριος. Μάθωμεν οὖν, ὅτι δι' ἀπο στροφὴν καὶ ἀμέλειαν ταύτας ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς τὰς πληγὰς ἐνίησιν, οὐκ ἐκτρῖψαι ζητῶν, ἀλλ' ἐπανορθῶσαι σπουδάζων, κατὰ τοὺς χρηστοὺς τῶν πατέρων καὶ ἀμελεῖς τῶν τέκνων, οἳ θυμοῦνται κατὰ τῶν νέων, καὶ διανίστανται, οὐ κακόν τι δοῦναι σπουδάζοντες. ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς νηπιώδους ὀλιγωρίας καὶ τῶν τῆς νεό τητος ἁμαρτιῶν εἰς ἐπιμέλειαν ἄγοντες. Ὁρᾶτε τοί νυν, ὡς τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἡμετέρων ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ τὰς ὥρας τῶν ἰδίων ἐξήγαγε φύσεων, καὶ τῶν καιρῶν τὰς ἰδέας εἰς ἀλλοκότους κράσεις διήμειψεν. Ὁ χειμὼν οὐκ ἔσχε τὸ σύνηθες ὑγρὸν μετὰ τοῦ ξηροῦ, ἀλλὰ πᾶσαν ἰκμάδα τῷ κρυστάλλῳ κατέδησέ τε καὶ ἀπεξήρανεν, ἄμοιρος δὲ διετέλεσε καὶ νιφάδων καὶ ὑετῶν. Τὸ ἔαρ πάλιν τὸ μὲν ἕτερον μέρος τῶν ἰδιωμάτων ἔδειξε, τὴν θερμότητα λέγω· τοῦ δὲ ὑγροῦ τὴν μετουσίαν οὐκ ἔσχε. Καῦμα δὲ καὶ κρυμὸς, καινῶς ὑπερβάντα τοὺς ὅρους τῆς κτίσεως, καὶ κακῶς εἰς τὴν καθ' ἡμῶν συμφωνήσαντα βλάβην, τοῦ βίου καὶ τῆς ζωῆς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐλαύνουσι. Τίς οὖν ἄρα τῆς ἀταξίας καὶ τῆς συγχύσεως ἡ αἰτία; τίς ὁ νεωτερισμὸς τῶν καιρῶν; Ἐρευνήσωμεν, ὡς νοῦν ἔχοντες· ὡς λογικοὶ, λογισώμεθα. Μὴ ὁ κυβερνῶν τὸ πᾶν οὐκ ἔστι; μὴ ὁ ἀριστοτέχνης Θεὸς ἐπελάθετο τῆς οἰκονομίας; μὴ ἀφῃρέθη τῆς ἐξουσίας καὶ τῆς δυνάμεως; ἢ τὴν ἰσχὺν μὲν τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχει, καὶ τοῦ κράτους οὐ παρελύθη· παρηνέχθη δὲ εἰς σκληρότητα, καὶ τὸ λίαν ἀγαθὸν, καὶ τὸ περὶ ἡμᾶς κηδεμονικὸν εἰς μισανθρωπίαν μετέβαλεν; Οὐκ ἂν εἴποι τις σωφρονῶν· ἀλλὰ φανερὰ καὶ δῆλα τὰ αἴτια δι' ἃ συνήθως οὐ διοικούμεθα. Λαμβάνοντες ἡμεῖς, ἄλλοις οὐ παρέχομεν· τὴν εὐεργεσίαν ἐπαινοῦμεν, καὶ ταύτης ἀποστεροῦμεν τοὺς δεομένους. Δοῦλοι ὄντες, ἐλευθερούμεθα, καὶ τοὺς ὁμοδούλους οὐκ οἰκτείρομεν· πεινῶντες τρεφόμεθα, καὶ τὸν ἐνδεῆ παρατρέχομεν. Ἀνενδεῆ χορηγὸν καὶ ταμίαν Θεὸν ἔχοντες, φειδωλοὶ ἐγενόμεθα καὶ ἀκοινώνητοι πρὸς τοὺς πένητας. Πολύτοκα ἡμῶν τὰ πρόβατα, καὶ οἱ γυμνοὶ τῶν προβάτων πλείους. Αἱ ἀποθῆκαι τῷ πλήθει τῶν ἀποκειμένων στενοῦνται, καὶ τὸν ἐστε νωμένον οὐκ ἐλεοῦμεν. Διὰ τοῦτο ἡμῖν ἀπειλεῖ τὸ δίκαιον κριτήριον. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ Θεὸς οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὴν χεῖρα, ἐπειδὴ τὴν φιλαδελφίαν ἡμεῖς ἀπεκλείσαμεν.
thought_title: The drought as God's corrective discipline for greed
orientation: Basil has just described the withered fields and now turns to the farmers' grief, then quotes Amos to show that the drought is God's response to the people's failure to turn back to him.
pass_a_gloss: The farmers, sitting upon the plowed fields and clasping their hands upon their knees (this indeed is the posture of mourners), weep over their vain labors, looking toward infant children and lamenting; gazing at wives and mourning, touching and feeling the dry stalks of the crops, and wailing loudly, just as fathers who have lost sons in the bloom of youth. Let it be said therefore also to us by the same prophet, whom a little earlier in the introduction we mentioned: And I, he says, withheld from you the rain before three months of the harvest; and I will rain upon one city, and upon one city I will not rain; and one portion will be rained upon, and the portion upon which I will not rain will be dried up. And two or three cities will gather together into one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied; because you did not turn back to me, says the Lord. Let us learn therefore that because of turning away and negligence God sends these blows upon us, not seeking to destroy us, but eager to set us right, like good fathers with careless children, who are angry with the young and rise up, not eager to give some evil, but leading them from childish neglect and the sins of youth to carefulness. You see therefore how the multitude of our sins has led the seasons out of their own natures, and has changed the forms of the times into strange mixtures. The winter did not have its customary moisture along with dryness, but bound up all dampness with ice and dried it out, and continued without share of snows and rains. The spring again showed one part of its properties, the warmth I mean; but it did not have the participation of moisture. Burning heat and frost, strangely overstepping the boundaries of creation, and badly conspiring together for harm against us, drive human beings out of life and living. What then is the cause of the disorder and the confusion? What is the innovation of the seasons? Let us search, as those who have understanding; as rational beings, let us reason. Is not the one who steers the universe present? Has the master-craftsman God forgotten his governance? Has he been stripped of authority and power? Or does he have the same strength, and has he not been weakened in might; but has he been carried away into harshness, and has he changed his exceeding goodness and his care for us into hatred of humanity? No one in his right mind would say so; but the causes through which we are not being governed in the usual way are clear and evident. We receive, but we do not provide to others; we praise the benefaction, and we deprive the needy of it. Being slaves, we are set free, and we do not pity our fellow slaves; being hungry, we are fed, and we pass by the one in want. Having God as a provider without need and a steward, we have become stingy and selfish toward the poor. Our sheep bear many young, and the naked are more numerous than the sheep. The storehouses are cramped by the multitude of stored goods, and we do not pity the one in distress. Because of this the just judgment seat threatens us. Because of this also God does not open his hand, since we have shut out love for one another.

choices.why: Glossary term for one who refuses to share; keeps the moral force of the refusal rather than a generic negative.
Glossary rendering for love shown to fellow Christians by sharing goods.
Captures the corrective, restorative purpose Basil emphasizes against the idea of destruction.
Keeps the spatial metaphor of turning from God, matching the Amos quotation's 'you did not turn back.'
Preserves the sense of a strange new departure in the seasons, which Basil treats as a violation of created order.
Renders the compound literally to preserve Basil's image of God as the supreme artisan of creation.

bible_refs.note: Καὶ ἐγὼ ἀνέσχον ἐξ ὑμῶν τὸν ὑετὸν πρὸ τριῶν μηνῶν τοῦ τρυγητοῦ· καὶ βρέξω ἐπὶ πόλιν μίαν, ἐπὶ δὲ πόλιν μίαν οὐ βρέξω· καὶ μερὶς μία βραχήσεται, καὶ μερὶς ἐφ' ἣν οὐ βρέξω ξηρανθήσεται. Καὶ συναθροίσονται δύο ἢ τρεῖς πόλεις εἰς μίαν πιεῖν ὕδωρ, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐμπλησθῶσι· διότι οὐκ ἐπεστράφητε πρὸς μέ, λέγει Κύριος.

pass_b_english: The farmers sit on their fields, clasping their hands over their knees—the very posture of mourners—and weep over their useless labors. They look at their little children and lament; they gaze at their wives and grieve; they touch and feel the dry stalks of their crops and cry out loudly, like fathers who have lost sons in the flower of youth. Let the same prophet I mentioned a moment ago in the introduction speak to us as well: “I withheld the rain from you three months before the harvest. I will send rain on one city, and on another city I will send no rain. One field will be soaked, and the field on which I send no rain will wither. Two or three cities will gather to one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied, because you did not turn back to me, says the Lord” (Amos 4:7-8). Let us learn, then, that God sends these blows upon us because of our turning away and neglect—not seeking to destroy us, but eager to set us right, like good fathers with careless children, who grow angry with the young and rise up against them, not because they are eager to do them harm, but to lead them from childish indifference and the sins of youth into careful living. You see, then, how the multitude of our sins has driven the seasons out of their own natures and changed the character of the times into strange mixtures. Winter did not have its usual moisture alongside the dry cold; instead the frost bound up and dried out every trace of dampness, and the season passed without snow or rain. Spring, in turn, displayed one part of its proper qualities—the warmth, I mean—but had no share of moisture. Scorching heat and biting cold, strangely overstepping the boundaries of creation and wickedly conspiring together for our harm, drive human beings from their livelihood and their very life. What, then, is the cause of this disorder and confusion? What is this innovation in the seasons? Let us search it out, as people with understanding; let us reason it through, as rational beings. Is there no one steering the universe? Has God the master-craftsman forgotten his governance? Has he been stripped of authority and power? Or does he still hold the same strength and has not lost his might, but has been carried away into harshness, and has turned his great goodness and care for us into hatred of humanity? No one in his right mind would say that. Rather, the causes are plain and clear, and they explain why we are not governed in the usual way. We receive, but we do not give to others. We praise generosity, and we rob the needy of it. We are slaves, and we are set free, yet we do not pity our fellow slaves. We are hungry, and we are fed, yet we pass by the one in want. We have God as a provider and steward who lacks nothing, yet we have become stingy and selfish toward the poor. Our sheep bear many young, and the naked are more numerous than the sheep. Our storehouses are cramped by the abundance of what is stored in them, and we do not pity the one in distress. This is why the righteous judgment threatens us. This is why God does not open his hand: because we have shut the door on love for one another.

last_rejected.quote: like good fathers with careless children, who grow angry with the young and rise up against them, not because they are eager to do them harm
last_rejected.source_quote: κατὰ τοὺς χρηστοὺς τῶν πατέρων καὶ ἀμελεῖς τῶν τέκνων, οἳ θυμοῦνται κατὰ τῶν νέων, καὶ διανίστανται, οὐ κακόν τι δοῦναι σπουδάζοντες
last_rejected.why: English says 'not because they are eager to do them harm' but source says 'not eager to give something bad'—the 'because' and 'to them' are added, changing syntax; 'δοῦναι' is 'to give' not 'to do.'
last_rejected.fix: not eager to inflict harm, but to lead them
last_rejected.ruling: δοῦναι κακόν = 'give/inflict harm'; 'do them harm' is valid dynamic rendering, not a major change.

last_rejected.source_quote: κακῶς εἰς τὴν καθ' ἡμῶν συμφωνήσαντα βλάβην
last_rejected.why: English 'wickedly conspiring together' suggests moral evil, but κακῶς here means 'badly, harmfully'—the elements are ill-coordinated for harm, not morally wicked.
last_rejected.ruling: κακῶς συμφωνήσαντα = 'wickedly/badly conspiring/agreeing together'; rendering within normal range, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: we are slaves, and we are set free
last_rejected.why: English 'we are set free' suggests manumission, but ἐλευθερούμεθα here is passive 'we are fed/supported' (from ἐλευθερόω in sense of 'set at liberty' from want), or possibly 'we are treated as free men.' The context of famine suggests 'we are provided for' or 'relieved.'
last_rejected.fix: we are slaves, yet we are set free from want
last_rejected.ruling: ἐλευθερούμεθα = 'we are set free'; standard meaning. Claimed alternative 'provided for' lacks lexical support.

last_rejected.quote: God does not open his hand
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ Θεὸς οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὴν χεῖρα
last_rejected.why: English loses the definite article and possessive: 'his hand' not 'the hand'—but more importantly, 'does not open his hand' misses that this is God's hand of bounty/giving, a biblical idiom.
last_rejected.fix: God does not open his hand
last_rejected.ruling: 'Does not open his hand' correctly renders οὐκ ἀνοίγει τὴν χεῖρα; possessive 'his' is natural English, idiom preserved.

last_rejected.quote: we have shut the door on love for one another
last_rejected.why: English 'shut the door on' adds metaphor not in source; ἀπεκλείσαμεν means 'we shut out, excluded, closed off'—not specifically 'shut the door on.'
last_rejected.fix: we have shut out love for one another
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπεκλείσαμεν = 'shut out/excluded'; 'shut the door on' is natural idiom within meaning range, not a major error.
